newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dependent Belgians to outnumber workers - report.
newsitem.headline: Dependent Belgians to outnumber workers - report.

text.p: Longer life spans and fewer babies in Belgium mean that after 2025 the number of those dependent on the state will outweigh those available for work, official figures released on Thursday showed.

The number of Belgians, put at 10.13 million on January 1, 1995, was projected to fall by just 1.5 percent to 9.98 million by the start of 2051 after peaking in 2020, a report by the National Statistics Office said.
Published jointly with the Planning Bureau, Belgium's government think-tank, the study will be used to help politicians consider future social security and pension needs.

Graphs showed that shortly after the turn of the century the population aged over 60 years as a percentage of the active population will be rising at a rate of one percent a year to reach 65 to 70 percent in 2050.
This compares with under 40 percent now and under 30 percent in 1950.
Include those aged under 20 and the dependent population as a percentage of those working will top 110 percent in 2050.
Of the 1995 total of 10 million, 24 percent were 19 or under and 21 percent 60 and over, while in 2025 the percentages were forecast at 21 percent and 32 percent respectively.
The average number of children per woman should actually rise to 1.75 in 2050 from 1.55 last year but the number of women aged 20 to 40 would continue to decline.
As a result the annual birth rate should fall 12.7 percent over the 55-year time span to 101,000 from 115,000.

A table on female mortality - women statistically outlive men - showed that on average they would be living about eight years longer in 2050 than in 1995 when the average age of death was 80.5 and 73.7 years for men.

The number of immigrants would fall to 60,000 from 61,000 while the number of emigrants would rise to 57,000 from 50,000. This meant the net influx of people in 1995 was 11,000, and should narrow to 3,000 in 2050.
